The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let \(v_p(n)\) denote the exponent of prime \(p\) in \(n\).

When Mark replaces \(a,b\) by \(\gcd(a,b)\) and \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\), for each prime \(p\) the two exponents
\[
v_p(a), v_p(b)
\]
become
\[
\min(v_p(a),v_p(b)),\ \max(v_p(a),v_p(b)).
\]
Thus for every prime \(p\), the multiset of \(p\)-exponents on the board is invariant.

At the final state, no move can change the multiset of numbers. If two numbers \(x,y\) were incomparable by divisibility, then
\[
\gcd(x,y)<x,y<\operatorname{lcm}(x,y),
\]
so replacing \(x,y\) by their gcd and lcm would change the multiset. Therefore, in the final state, the numbers form a chain under divisibility:
\[
F_1\mid F_2\mid \cdots \mid F_{2100}.
\]
This is also the nondecreasing order of the numbers on the board.

For each prime \(p\), the sequence
\[
v_p(F_1),v_p(F_2),\dots,v_p(F_{2100})
\]
is nondecreasing and has the same multiset as
\[
v_p(1),v_p(2),\dots,v_p(2100).
\]
So \(v_p(F_{2026})\) is the \(2026\)-th smallest \(p\)-exponent among \(1,2,\dots,2100\), equivalently the \(75\)-th largest such exponent, since
\[
2100-2026+1=75.
\]

For a prime \(p\), the number of integers \(n\le 2100\) with \(v_p(n)\ge t\) is
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^t}\right\rfloor.
\]
Thus \(v_p(F_{2026})\) is the largest \(t\) such that
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^t}\right\rfloor\ge 75.
\]
Since \(2100=75\cdot 28\), this is equivalent to
\[
p^t\le 28.
\]

So we need the largest power of each prime not exceeding \(28\):

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}
p & 2 & 3 & 5 & 7 & 11 & 13 & 17 & 19 & 23 \\
\hline
v_p(F_{2026}) & 4 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1
\end{array}
\]

All other primes have exponent \(0\). Hence
\[
F_{2026}=2^4\cdot 3^3\cdot 5^2\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 19\cdot 23.
\]

The number of positive divisors is
\[
(4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^6
=5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 64
=3840.
\]

\[
\boxed{3840}
\]
